title: Janapada of Avanti
capsule: During the window of c. 600–404 BCE, Avanti was one of the most powerful of the sixteen Mahajanapadas of early India, occupying the Malwa plateau and divided by the Vindhya range into a northern half centered on Ujjayinī (Ujjain) and a southern half on the Narmada at Māhiṣmatī. It was ruled by the Pradyota dynasty, whose founder Pradyota—remembered in Pali Buddhist sources as Caṇḍa Pajjota, 'Pradyota the Fierce'—was a contemporary of the Buddha and of Bimbisāra and Ajātaśatru of Magadha, and was strong enough to be reckoned one of the four great powers of northern India. Pradyota's rivalry with the Vatsa king Udayana is a staple of later Sanskrit drama, and his successors continued to rule from Ujjayinī, a major node on the trade routes linking the Gangetic plain to the western port of Bharukaccha. Toward the close of this window the Pradyota line was extinguished by Śiśunāga of Magadha (c. 413 BCE), absorbing Avanti into the expanding Magadhan state.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The northern and southern divisions and their capitals are textually secure, but the precise extent of Avanti's borders at any given period is approximate, reconstructed from the Purāṇas and Pāli sources.
